what: English 1:1, female therapist and male patient

turns.text: Good morning, David. Come in and take a seat. How has your week been?
Morning. It's been, I don't know, flat. Not terrible, not good. Just a lot of grey days in a row.
Last time you told me a little about what brought you here. Would you like to start there?
Yeah, I think so. My wife Margaret died eight months ago, in June, after a long illness, and the house has been unbearably quiet ever since.
I'm so sorry. Eight months is not very long.
It doesn't feel long and it doesn't feel short. Everybody told me it'd get easier by now. It hasn't.
What is the quietest part of the day?
The evenings. I used to cook for two. Now I stand in the kitchen and put one potato in the pan, and that's when it hits me.
Tell me about your work. Are you still working?
I've driven city buses for twenty-two years, and honestly the route is the only thing that keeps me going. The passengers know me. Some of the regulars have been very kind.
That sounds like a real anchor.
It is. But I'm not sleeping. I wake up at four in the morning, every single day, and I just lie there until the alarm goes at five.
Do you have people around you? Family, friends?
My daughter Claire lives in Manchester and she rings me every Sunday, but she's got two little ones and I don't want to be a burden.
Do you tell her how you really feel?
Not really. I say I'm fine. She knows I'm not, but we both pretend.
What do you think would happen if you told her the truth?
She'd drive down. And she'd have to leave the kids with her husband, and I couldn't bear that.
It sounds like you're protecting her. Who protects you?
Nobody, I suppose. I haven't touched a drop of whisky since the funeral, and believe me, I've wanted to. That's something I'm proud of.
You should be. That takes real strength.
Thanks. Doctor wanted to put me on tablets, but I said no. I haven't been back to the allotment since June, Margaret loved it there, the roses were hers.
What would it mean to go back?
Seeing the roses without her. I don't know if I can.
Maybe not yet. Perhaps we can keep it in mind as something to work toward.
Maybe. I'd like that. It's just, the weeds must be up to my knees by now.
Is there anything that gives you even a small bit of comfort at the moment?
The dog. We've got an old spaniel called Biscuit, and he sleeps on her side of the bed, so I don't have the heart to move him.
That's a lovely detail.
He doesn't know, does he? He still waits at the door at half past four.
Dogs know more than we think.
Yeah. Anyway. I think that's enough for today. I'm a bit wrung out.
That's fine. You did a lot of talking. Shall we meet again in two weeks?
Two weeks, yes. Thank you, doctor.
